$comment: Worked examples are DATA, traceable to a named source (REQUIREMENTS.md §11). Each carries the values its book reports and the tolerance it reports them to, so `src/data/examples.test.ts` can grade the engine against the book rather than against itself. A tolerance is part of the citation: a book that prints 47.9 kJ/kg is not claiming 47.9087.

examples.title: Saturated air at 25 °C, sea level
examples.teaches: At saturation, relative humidity and degree of saturation coincide — and only there. Away from the curve they part company, which is why the panel shows both.

examples.title: Room air at 24 °C, 50% RH
examples.teaches: The standard comfort state. Relative humidity reads 50% and degree of saturation 49.2% — three quarters of a point apart, at the state a designer uses most.

examples.title: 24 °C, 50% RH at 1609 m
examples.teaches: The same temperature and relative humidity at Denver's elevation carries over 20% more moisture, because humidity ratio depends on barometric pressure. This is why elevation is an input to every calculation and not a refinement.

examples.title: −10 °C at 60% RH
examples.source: IAPWS-06 sublimation line; ASHRAE Handbook—Fundamentals, Ch. 1
examples.teaches: Below freezing the saturation line runs over ice, so the dew point is a FROST point and the wet bulb is sub-freezing too. A Magnus fit carried below zero overstates the saturation pressure by more than 20% here.
